When is the best time to get your flu shot? WCVB US LIVE Current Time 0:00 / Total Duration 3:26 Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Advertisement Updated: 6:54 AM PDT Oct 2, 2026 Editorial Standards i By By Jacqueline Howard, CNN Respiratory virus season has arrived. Here’s what to know about flu, Covid-19 and RSV vaccines this fall Updated: 6:54 AM PDT Oct 2, 2026 Editorial Standards i By By Jacqueline Howard, CNN There’s a bit of a chill in the air, pumpkin spice in your coffee and children back to school — which means the threat of respiratory viruses like Covid-19, influenza and RSV is looming. Some respiratory illnesses have arrived already. Seasonal influenza activity is still low at the national level, data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows. Advertisement But certain flu metrics are inching up – especially in the West . Health officials in Washington state’s King County note that since mid-August there has been an increase in people with flu visiting emergency departments in the area. Related video above | When is the best time to get your flu shot? Vaccines that help prevent illness and reduce the risk of serious infections and hospitalization are now available, and for some people, this is the right time to roll up their sleeves. Typically, the CDC launches a fall campaign around this time of year, recommending seasonal immunizations such as the flu shot and Covid-19 vaccines. But after sweeping changes to the agency’s vaccine advisory committee during the second Trump administration and ongoing lawsuits, the CDC recently posted guidance online to follow last year’s recommendations for flu and Covid-19. Meanwhile, the American Medical Association and the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project launched their own independent reviews of this fall’s vaccines – including those for flu , Covid and RSV – which were published in September in the medical journal JAMA. The review papers helped inform 2026-27 respiratory virus immunization recommendations released by several medical groups, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Infectious Diseases Society of America. Flu and COVID-19 vaccines are rolling out, but one shot is still not available “For more than 60 years, the United States has benefited from an established federal process for evaluating vaccine evidence and translating that science into recommendations for the American public. At the center of that process were the Centers for Disease Control and its Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the ACIP,” Dr. Bruce Gellin, board chair of the Vaccine Integrity Project and professor of medicine at Georgetown University, said at a news briefing. “Unfortunately today, the federal government is not fulfilling that responsibility in the way that it historically has. But the need for that work has not disappeared. Influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and the RSV viruses will circulate again this fall and winter,” Gellin said. “Clinicians will still have patients to care for. Parents will still have decisions to make for their children, and older Americans, pregnant women and people with underlying health conditions will still need to know how best to protect themselves,” he said. “We cannot allow the breakdown of a federal process to create a vacuum in evidence-based vaccine guidance.” The US Department of Health and Human Services has not responded to CNN’s request for comment on the groups’ recommendations. Flu, Covid-19 and RSV immunizations are now available at most major pharmacies. “And really reassuringly, insurers have indicated to the major groups that they will cover these respiratory virus immunizations,” Dr. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, said in a news briefing. Ordering through Vaccines for Children, the federal program that provides routine immunizations at no cost to children who are uninsured or underinsured or whose families may not otherwise be able to afford them, has also started. About half of US children are eligible for the program. “Vaccines are one of medicine’s greatest success stories. They prevent serious illness, reduce hospitalizations and long-term complications and save lives,” Nosal said in a news release. “As federal guidance evolves, the science behind vaccines remains strong. These recommendations are grounded in the latest evidence, informed by public health experts and shaped by what family physicians are seeing every day in their patients.” Why people who qualify should get the RSV vaccine RSV immunization Who should get it The groups eligible for RSV immunizations include older adults, pregnant people and infants. “People age 50 and older with high-risk conditions, and everyone over 75 years old, should get one dose,” Nosal said. “This is not an annual vaccine. If you got one before, you do not need a new one this year. Getting one should protect you throughout the entire season.” During pregnancy, RSV vaccination is recommended in the third trimester, between weeks 32 and 36. Children younger than 8 months should be immunized against RSV using a monoclonal antibody unless their mother got an RSV vaccination during pregnancy, said Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics. “If the mother’s immunization status is unknown, that child should be immunized,” Racine said in the briefing. He added that children between 8 months and 19 months of age who are in certain high-risk groups for severe disease are also recommended to get the RSV monoclonal antibody. And a single dose of RSV vaccine is recommended for adults who have weakened immune systems. “Immunosuppressed individuals are at higher risk for severe disease than immunocompetent individuals,” Dr. Dan Barouch, director of the Center for Virology and Vaccine Research at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, who was not involved in the new recommendations, said in an email. “The vaccines are also generally less effective in immunosuppressed individuals compared with immunocompetent individuals.” When to get it For older adults, RSV vaccinations are typically recommended in late summer and early fall. The advice slightly changed this year for pregnant people. “ACOG now recommends that pregnant individuals receive a single dose of the maternal RSV vaccine, Abrysvo, from September 1 through March 1 instead of only through January 31,” Dr. Christina Davidson, chief medical officer of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, said in the news briefing. “We made this change because the RSV disease season is now occurring later in the spring, and it is also more severe than it used to be,” Davidson said. “The extension of the eligibility window will help provide pregnant patients and their infants with additional protection.” For infants, the RSV monoclonal antibody is typically recommended around virus season, from October through March. Seasonal flu shots Who should get it Everyone 6 months and older is recommended to get an annual flu shot. “On average, flu vaccines reduce the risk of needing to go to the doctor by 30% to 60%,” Nosal said. “Adults 65 years and older should get an enhanced flu vaccine, one that is high-dose, adjuvanted or recombinant, when it’s available,” she said. “But do not delay your vaccination if that one’s not available.” And for the first time, an mRNA-based flu vaccine is available for use in adults 50 and older. The flu vaccine is also recommended during pregnancy, but pregnant people should avoid the nasal spray version, according to the recommendations. “Pregnant and postpartum people still have a significantly higher risk of developing serious complications from infection compared with non-pregnant people,” Davidson said. “The inactivated or recombinant influenza vaccines remain the only vaccines that are recommended for use in pregnancy in any trimester, so please work with your OB care clinician or pharmacist to get these,” she said. “Most importantly, if you are able to get the vaccine while you are pregnant, the immunity will also, in part, pass on to your baby.” When to get it October is the ideal time to get vaccinated, Nolan said, because “protection wanes throughout the season.” Some providers use the slogan “ flu before boo ” to remind people to get a flu shot before Halloween. Updated Covid-19 vaccines Who should get it Getting an updated Covid-19 vaccine is recommended for adults. “If you’re older than 19, we recommend getting the Covid-19 vaccine,” Nosal said. “This is especially important for people who are 65 years and older, at increased risk for severe Covid infection and those who’ve never received a Covid-19 vaccine,” she said. “For those adults 65 years and older, they should receive a second dose of the updated Covid-19 vaccine six months after that season’s initial dose to help maintain protection as immunity wanes over time.” The vaccine is also recommended for infants between 6 months and 23 months of age, and children in certain high-risk groups or those whose families request vaccination. And for people who are immunocompromised, the annual updated Covid-19 vaccine is recommended for ages 6 months and older. Last year, the CDC recommended Covid-19 vaccines based on conversations with the patient’s healthcare provider, known as shared decision-making, Barouch noted, but the agency “also emphasized that the risk-benefit of the vaccines is most favorable for individuals who are at higher risk of severe disease.” Davidson, of ACOG, said the vaccine is also recommended during pregnancy. “The most important message is this: If you are pregnant, considering pregnancy or are a new or breastfeeding parent, please get your vaccine or your annual booster. All four of the available Covid vaccines are safe for you,” Davidson said. Moderna offers two mRNA shots, Pfizer and BioNTech have another, and Sanofi and Novavax offer a more traditional protein-based version. “A recommendation for the Covid vaccine is based on more than five years of research and millions of administered doses,” Davidson said. “I want to emphasize that the evidence has found no increased risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth or birth defects. The risks of complications from Covid for pregnant people and their babies, however, are high. So please get the vaccine.” When to get it It’s recommended to get the updated vaccine now, but if you have been recently infected with Covid, experts advise waiting four to six months before getting the vaccine. The updated Covid-19 vaccine “targets the most recent strain that’s been circulating, and so if you want to update your protection, that’s the best way to do it,” Dr. Sandra Adamson Fryhofer, president-elect of the American Medical Association, said in a news briefing. “You know, your computer constantly needs to be updated. Well, your immune system, your immunity needs to be constantly updated too,” she said. “You’re going to get your most protection in those first few months after the vaccine. So if you have a big event – if you have to go to a wedding, or if you’re going on some fabulous trip, or you’re going to a fabulous birthday party, or just any birthday party or get-together – think about getting that vaccine a couple of weeks before that event, so you’ll stay healthy and well.” Make KCRA a preferred source on Google Add Preferred Source Infinite Scroll Enabled Top Picks Robert Kelker-Kelly, former star of ‘Days of Our Lives,’ ‘General Hospital’ and ‘Another World,’ has died, reports say California voter guide 2026: What to know about the propositions and races on the November ballot Trump draws backlash after he suggests Iran could 'take out' Los Angeles or San Diego 'Soundtrack to our love stories': R&B singer Freddie Jackson dies at 69 SPONSORED CONTENT Spinal Stenosis Isn't an Age Problem - The Real Cause May Surprise You SmoothSpine 98% of Americans Are Using Toxic Frying Pans - The Chefs Are Doing This Now Plateful He Installed This Hummingbird House. He added that children between 8 months and 19 months of age who are in certain high-risk groups for severe disease are also recommended to get the RSV monoclonal antibody. And a single dose of RSV vaccine is recommended for adults who have weakened immune systems. “Immunosuppressed individuals are at higher risk for severe disease than immunocompetent individuals,” Dr. Dan Barouch, director of the Center for Virology and Vaccine Research at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, who was not involved in the new recommendations, said in an email. “The vaccines are also generally less effective in immunosuppressed individuals compared with immunocompetent individuals.” When to get it For older adults, RSV vaccinations are typically recommended in late summer and early fall. The advice slightly changed this year for pregnant people. “ACOG now recommends that pregnant individuals receive a single dose of the maternal RSV vaccine, Abrysvo, from September 1 through March 1 instead of only through January 31,” Dr. Christina Davidson, chief medical officer of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, said in the news briefing. “We made this change because the RSV disease season is now occurring later in the spring, and it is also more severe than it used to be,” Davidson said. “The extension of the eligibility window will help provide pregnant patients and their infants with additional protection.” For infants, the RSV monoclonal antibody is typically recommended around virus season, from October through March. Seasonal flu shots Who should get it Everyone 6 months and older is recommended to get an annual flu shot. “On average, flu vaccines reduce the risk of needing to go to the doctor by 30% to 60%,” Nosal said. “Adults 65 years and older should get an enhanced flu vaccine, one that is high-dose, adjuvanted or recombinant, when it’s available,” she said. “But do not delay your vaccination if that one’s not available.” And for the first time, an mRNA-based flu vaccine is available for use in adults 50 and older. The flu vaccine is also recommended during pregnancy, but pregnant people should avoid the nasal spray version, according to the recommendations. “Pregnant and postpartum people still have a significantly higher risk of developing serious complications from infection compared with non-pregnant people,” Davidson said. “The inactivated or recombinant influenza vaccines remain the only vaccines that are recommended for use in pregnancy in any trimester, so please work with your OB care clinician or pharmacist to get these,” she said. “Most importantly, if you are able to get the vaccine while you are pregnant, the immunity will also, in part, pass on to your baby.” When to get it October is the ideal time to get vaccinated, Nolan said, because “protection wanes throughout the season.” Some providers use the slogan “ flu before boo ” to remind people to get a flu shot before Halloween. Updated Covid-19 vaccines Who should get it Getting an updated Covid-19 vaccine is recommended for adults. “If you’re older than 19, we recommend getting the Covid-19 vaccine,” Nosal said. “This is especially important for people who are 65 years and older, at increased risk for severe Covid infection and those who’ve never received a Covid-19 vaccine,” she said. “For those adults 65 years and older, they should receive a second dose of the updated Covid-19 vaccine six months after that season’s initial dose to help maintain protection as immunity wanes over time.” The vaccine is also recommended for infants between 6 months and 23 months of age, and children in certain high-risk groups or those whose families request vaccination. And for people who are immunocompromised, the annual updated Covid-19 vaccine is recommended for ages 6 months and older. Last year, the CDC recommended Covid-19 vaccines based on conversations with the patient’s healthcare provider, known as shared decision-making, Barouch noted, but the agency “also emphasized that the risk-benefit of the vaccines is most favorable for individuals who are at higher risk of severe disease.” Davidson, of ACOG, said the vaccine is also recommended during pregnancy. “The most important message is this: If you are pregnant, considering pregnancy or are a new or breastfeeding parent, please get your vaccine or your annual booster. All four of the available Covid vaccines are safe for you,” Davidson said. Moderna offers two mRNA shots, Pfizer and BioNTech have another, and Sanofi and Novavax offer a more traditional protein-based version. “A recommendation for the Covid vaccine is based on more than five years of research and millions of administered doses,” Davidson said. “I want to emphasize that the evidence has found no increased risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth or birth defects. The risks of complications from Covid for pregnant people and their babies, however, are high. So please get the vaccine.” When to get it It’s recommended to get the updated vaccine now, but if you have been recently infected with Covid, experts advise waiting four to six months before getting the vaccine. The updated Covid-19 vaccine “targets the most recent strain that’s been circulating, and so if you want to update your protection, that’s the best way to do it,” Dr. Sandra Adamson Fryhofer, president-elect of the American Medical Association, said in a news briefing. “You know, your computer constantly needs to be updated. Well, your immune system, your immunity needs to be constantly updated too,” she said. “You’re going to get your most protection in those first few months after the vaccine. So if you have a big event – if you have to go to a wedding, or if you’re going on some fabulous trip, or you’re going to a fabulous birthday party, or just any birthday party or get-together – think about getting that vaccine a couple of weeks before that event, so you’ll stay healthy and well.” Infinite Scroll Enabled Top Picks Authorities identify 2 killed in Mississippi River boating accident near Dubuque Robert Kelker-Kelly, former star of ‘Days of Our Lives,’ ‘General Hospital’ and ‘Another World,’ has died, reports say President Trump approves rare firing squad execution for Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan Teacher who sued Iowa school district for students’ ‘racist’ acts, language wins $425,000 SPONSORED CONTENT Spinal Stenosis Isn't an Age Problem - The Real Cause May Surprise You SmoothSpine You'll Never Guess Which Common Item Helps Stop Your Dog's Itching & Scratching Pets Daily Health California: Worst Car Insurance Companies for Overcharging (Is Yours on The List?) records.content: Oriol Güell Barcelona - OCT 02, 2026 - 04:40 EDT Share on Whatsapp Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Prefer EL PAÍS on Google Compartir: Whatsapp Facebook Twitter Bluesky Linkedin Copy link A comprehensive atlas of the 18 main respiratory viruses circulating in Catalonia, produced for the first time in Spain by researchers from that northeastern region, reveals that the coronavirus that caused the Covid-16 pandemic — SARS-CoV-2 — “is currently not a winter virus. In recent years, it has shown clear peaks during the spring and summer, which is different from what was initially expected.” This behavior has caused a clear mismatch with the current vaccination calendar . “We are immunizing at-risk groups [older people, those with chronic illnesses...] in the autumn, when the virus’ epidemic waves have already passed, and not beforehand, as would be desirable. This work raises the possibility that it may be necessary to adjust the planning of vaccination campaigns and guidelines,” warns Jacobo Mendioroz, deputy director general for Surveillance and Public Health of the Catalan government. The research’s findings, based on Catalonia’s healthcare system data between 2022 and 2025, have been observed this year again in the real world. Coronavirus incidence surged at the end of summer, when communities had not yet begun the vaccination campaign against this pathogen, which is administered alongside the flu shot. The new research highlights SARS-CoV-2’s behavior, more erratic after the pandemic but now showing mainly “a clear summer epidemic pattern .” Juan Carlos Galán, head of Virology at Ramón y Cajal Hospital in Madrid, considers the research highly relevant but says it is still too early to classify the coronavirus as exclusively a summer virus: “There are recent data from other European countries, and some areas of Spain, that point more to a biennial incidence, in summer and winter. What was observed in Catalonia over these three seasons indicates a trend in SARS-CoV-2 behavior, but we do not know whether other viral or environmental factors could have impacted that finding and we will have to wait for the next seasons to confirm it.” This expert highlights the study’s contribution to a “fascinating field” he calls viral ecology. “We see that there are interferences and, at times, what appears to be competition among different viruses. A good example was the first year of the pandemic, when influenza disappeared completely, overwhelmed by covid. This apparent antagonism between flu and SARS-CoV-2 is observed in subsequent years. Each virus unfolds on the calendar in an orderly way, as if occupying different niches. Many factors intervene in this process, even if they are not fully understood,” he concludes. Changing vaccination campaigns For Gregorio Montes Salas, secretary general of the Spanish Society of Preventive Medicine, Public Health and Healthcare Management (SEMPSPGS), the study confirms that “the coronavirus has not followed the expected winter pattern, at least so far.” He adds that this raises the option of “considering the possibility of de-seasonalizing vaccination against SARS-CoV-2.” Mendioroz and Montes Salas agree that before making decisions “it will be necessary to wait for further research,” given the logistical complexity of changing campaigns and the risk of undermining achieved coverage (65% for flu among those 65 and older and 50% for coronavirus). The underlying idea is that, even if belated, it is preferable for at-risk people to be immunized by taking advantage of the momentum of regional autumn campaigns rather than spreading doses across the year and losing adherence. “Campaigns make mass vaccination easier. Changing dates requires a logistical effort that must be carefully studied, but it may be something worth exploring,” Montes Salas says. “The whole organization, the messaging and even public perception would change. The risk is that coverage could drop: who is going to get vaccinated at the start of summer against a virus that has always been associated with cold weather?” adds Mendioroz. The paper was published in the latest issue of Eurosurveillance — the scientific journal of the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) — and its main aim was to obtain a detailed picture of respiratory virus circulation. “Influenza has always been monitored and, more recently, Covid and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). But what about the others? The answer provides key information: it helps plan prevention measures, prepare health centers or hospitals for peaks in demand and even anticipate what might happen,” Mendioroz says. One reason this is possible, the study’s conclusions argue, is that “respiratory viruses mainly follow a predictable pattern, appearing one after another in a consistent order every year.” “We know, for example, that the flu wave is successively preceded by a rhinovirus wave and then a parainfluenza wave,” the Generalitat’s deputy director general for Surveillance illustrates. The researchers analyzed more than 33,000 samples obtained between October 2022 and September 2025 by the Information System for Infection Surveillance in Catalonia (SIVIC), the sentinel network that monitors respiratory viruses in real time. The panel tracks the following viruses and subtypes: three influenza A strains and one B, two RSV strains, SARS-CoV-2, two seasonal coronaviruses (NL63 and OC43), four parainfluenza types, and one each of the following groups: rhinovirus, enterovirus, adenovirus, metapneumovirus and bocavirus. Influenza A shows the clearest seasonal pattern, according to the paper. Its peak usually occurs in Spain between late December and early February, although most often it happens in the second half of January. “Meanwhile, influenza B displays a less regular seasonality” and is usually offset from that peak, the researchers conclude. RSV also has a clear winter pattern, although in this case it precedes the flu by a few weeks and typically “reaches its peak roughly a month before it.” Rhinoviruses and enteroviruses, which cause mild cold-like illnesses, instead show a two-wave pattern, with peaks in autumn (September–October) and spring. Rhinovirus circulation also “declines when SARS-CoV-2 is circulating strongly,” the paper notes. Another group of pathogens that infect the respiratory tract maintains a very different profile and shows a constant presence “throughout the year, without clearly defined epidemic peaks.” This is the case for adenoviruses, some coronaviruses other than SARS-CoV-2 (such as NL63) and two parainfluenza types (1 and 4). The study also details the sequence of the remaining pathogens: parainfluenza virus 2 slightly precedes influenza, while metapneumovirus — a pathogen very common in childhood — and parainfluenza 3 emerge just as influenza begins to decline. Meanwhile, bocavirus and the seasonal coronavirus OC43 begin activity in mid-autumn, but their incidence rises slowly to reach peaks between February and April. Understanding the warning older adults often hear during cold and flu season 7-minute read By Donna Shryer, AARP Published October 05, 2026 Kyle Hilton Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Add AARP as a preferred source on Google At the start of every flu season, Americans hear a familiar warning: Older adults and people with certain health conditions are at higher risk for respiratory viruses like COVID, flu and RSV. But what does “higher risk” actually mean — and what should you do with that information? More Ways to Benefit View All MEMBERS ONLY View Benefit MEMBERS ONLY View Benefit MEMBERS ONLY View Benefit MEMBERS ONLY View Benefit MEMBERS ONLY View Benefit 1 of 5 Previous Next Related Benefit 1 Related Benefit 2 Related Benefit 3 Related Benefit 4 Related Benefit 5 It’s about outcomes For most people, being at higher risk is less about catching a virus and more about what happens if you get an infection. If you’re at higher risk and you come down with the flu, COVID or RSV, you may be more likely to have a serious outcome, such as hospitalization, a stay in the ICU or even death. “By ‘severe disease,’ we mean ‘illness serious enough to get you hospitalized,’ ” says Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of preventive medicine and infectious diseases at Vanderbilt University School of Medicine in Nashville, Tennessee. “Hospitalization is the Rubicon. If you cross that, you’ve had severe disease.” Several factors can bump a person into a higher-risk category, from lifestyle habits, like smoking, to certain medical conditions that can complicate an infection or recovery from one. For example, people with diabetes face higher odds of a severe outcome from a respiratory infection than people without diabetes. There are also factors that can lower a person’s risk of severe illness, such as being vaccinated. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) apply the higher-risk label to conditions conclusively shown to increase the odds of a severe outcome, though that risk may vary from person to person. Individual risk is hard to communicate on a grand scale, says Dr. Kisha Davis, president-elect of the American Academy of Family Physicians. The label’s real job, she adds, is to tell you to take extra precautions. “It’s kind of like the yellow signal: Slow down, be a little bit more cautious,” Davis says. Age is the biggest risk factor for severe illness Of all the risk factors, age matters most. During the 2024-25 flu season, adults 65 and older accounted for 57 percent of flu hospitalizations and 71 percent of flu deaths. One major reason is that the immune system changes with age. The aging immune system takes longer to recognize a virus, says Dawn Bowdish, a professor of medicine at McMaster University and director of the Firestone Institute for Respiratory Health in Hamilton, Ontario. It doesn’t take weeks longer but hours, maybe a day. And that gives the virus a head start. When the virus is recognized, the body’s emergency response — inflammation — rushes immune cells and fluid to the trouble spot. With age, inflammation can overreact. Most Popular ARTICLE CONTINUES AFTER ADVERTISEMENT “Once it gets going, one of the big problems is there’s almost too much inflammation,” Bowdish says. That can flood the lungs with fluid, which is how a respiratory infection can turn into pneumonia. Inflammation is also slow to shut off, she adds, which is why an older adult can feel sick even as the infection subsides. Get More From AARP MEMBERS ONLY View MEMBERS ONLY View MEMBERS ONLY View The heart, lungs and kidneys age too. A younger body can better absorb the strain of a serious infection — the racing heart, labored breathing, dehydration. An older body is working closer to its limits before the virus arrives. And yes, this is true even if you are in top shape. “As a 75-year-old, I don’t care how many pull-ups you can do. You are at greater risk than a 40-year-old,” Schaffner says. 6 questions to ask your doctor about risk Do I have any health conditions that put me at higher risk for a severe outcome? Which vaccines do I need this fall? Do any of my medications put me in the higher-risk group? If I test positive for flu or COVID, am I a candidate for antiviral medicine? If so, how do I start it quickly? Which over-the-counter medicines should I avoid, and what should I keep on hand? What symptoms require a call to my health care provider? Common health conditions also affect risk Chronic conditions add to the risk. The CDC names several, including chronic lung disease, heart disease, diabetes and chronic kidney disease. These conditions can leave the body with less reserve to handle the added stress of an infection. Lungs already scarred by chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) have less healthy tissue to spare. Kidneys already struggling have little left to give. This is a warning for nearly every older adult. In 2023, 93 percent of adults 65 and older reported at least one chronic condition. Obesity can raise risk through more than one route. Extra weight affects how well the lungs work, and the low-grade inflammation that comes with excess fat tissue leaves the immune system running hot before infection even starts. Being immunocompromised — meaning your body can’t fight infections as easily as it should — also drives risk. Some chronic conditions weaken the immune system. So can certain drugs used to treat them, including prednisone and the biologics prescribed for rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn’s disease and psoriasis. These drugs are designed to tamp down the immune system, Davis says, to help prevent the complications of a chronic disease. But that also affects how the body responds to everything else and can leave you more susceptible to respiratory illness. No single health condition outranks the rest, Davis says. “I think they all worry me when they’re out of control,” she adds — which is why managing them is key. Picture: Ajkerpatrika More than 635,000 people were admitted to government hospitals in Bangladesh with fever, pneumonia and respiratory tract infections between the start of the year and September 24, amid continuing measles and dengue outbreaks, government data showed. Men outnumbered women among pneumonia and respiratory infection patients, while women accounted for a higher share of fever admissions. Excluding measles, measles symptoms and dengue, 635,000-plus patients were admitted with the three illnesses during the period. The total included 327,000 men and 308,000 women. Fever Data from the Directorate General of Health Services showed that unspecified or common fever was the most prevalent type among fever cases reported nationwide. Of around 395,000 fever patients, about 250,000 had unspecified fever. More than 130,000 people were admitted with fever of unknown origin, while 9,000 were hospitalised with specified fever and 842 with fever caused by drug side effects. Women accounted for 52% of fever patients, or 206,464 cases, compared with 188,784 men, or 48%. Doctors said female hormones, including oestrogen, can activate immune responses against viruses more rapidly, leading to stronger inflammation and fever symptoms. The pattern varies by age group. The highest number of fever cases was reported among one-year-old children, with about 28,500 cases. Pneumonia A total of 175,175 people were admitted to hospitals with pneumonia this year. The figure included 102,000 male patients and 73,000 female patients. Men also outnumbered women in admissions for pneumonia caused by respiratory viruses, adenoviruses, parainfluenza viruses, and Streptococcus and Haemophilus bacteria. Respiratory tract infections Hospitals admitted 64,775 patients with respiratory tract infections this year, including 35,797 men, or about 55%, and 28,958 women. Men were more numerous among patients with acute lower respiratory tract infections, acute bronchitis and acute nasal inflammation. Women, however, were more affected by acute inflammation of the tonsils. Public health experts said the gender differences in fever, pneumonia and respiratory tract infections were consistent with international public health research and Bangladesh’s context. Case-control studies by the United States Department of Health and Human Services’ Library of Medicine, the American Society for Microbiology and the Global Burden of Disease project have found that men are more likely to suffer from pneumonia and acute respiratory infections. Experts cited biological and social factors. Men may be more susceptible to bacterial and viral infections because of average lung structure and biological characteristics of their immune systems. In Bangladesh, men are also more likely to be exposed to dust, public transport and air pollution caused by unplanned urbanisation while working outside. Higher smoking rates among men can directly reduce lung function and substantially increase pneumonia risk. Public health experts also said higher male hospital admissions may reflect social patterns, as families often seek treatment more quickly when men fall ill, whereas women may receive medical care only after their condition becomes severe. A 2024 study published in the German-British scientific journal Springer Nature found gender differences in healthcare-seeking behaviour in South Asia, including Bangladesh. Biological and social gender influences affect access to and use of healthcare, as well as healthcare quality and financing. Senior public health specialist Dr Abu Jamil Faisal told Ajker Patrika: “There is no single reason why the number of male patients is higher in fever, pneumonia and respiratory tract infections. Greater exposure among men to air pollution, dust, workplace risks and smoking may be involved, while some biological differences in the immune system may also play a role. However, hospital admission data cannot determine the actual prevalence of diseases. Treatment-seeking behaviour and access to healthcare also affect such statistics.” The Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research, or IEDCR, has also been monitoring the gender disparity. The government agency, which monitors and controls epidemic, communicable and non-communicable diseases and conducts related research, collected patient samples from 10 specialised government hospitals and analysed infection trends by age, gender and disease type. IEDCR observations this year indicate the detection of respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, among respiratory infection cases. RSV is a contagious respiratory virus that can infect the nose, throat and lungs and is particularly significant among children. The institute has also observed differences in infection patterns between men and women. IEDCR Director Dr Kazi Ahmed Jaki told Ajker Patrika: “Whether it is influenza or RSV, we review it by age and gender. The first reason is that an infected person has come into contact with another infected person in some way. In cases of avian influenza or bird flu, there may have been contact with infected or dead birds, including domestic ducks, chickens or wild birds. The issue cannot be explained simply by saying that men are more affected by pneumonia or RTIs because they work outside.” Hospitals have faced additional pressure this year due to dengue and an unprecedented measles outbreak. More than 88,360 people had been admitted with dengue nationwide from the beginning of the year until Monday, while 271 people had died, according to Directorate General of Health Services statistics. A review of dengue data from this year and previous years showed that men accounted for more hospital admissions, but women accounted for more deaths. In 2023, men made up 60.1% of dengue admissions, while women accounted for 57% of deaths. The nationwide measles outbreak, which began in March, has also placed heavy pressure on hospitals. More than 219,000 people were identified with measles or measles symptoms between March 15 and October 5, and more than 175,000 of them were admitted to hospitals. Most of the more than 1,128 deaths were children. As a result, treatment plans cannot be based on only one specific disease. Patients with different infections must be managed at the same time, particularly with pressure from paediatric patients. In this situation, it is important to monitor patients according to their physical condition and symptoms, conduct necessary tests and begin treatment quickly.” Dengue patients in Mugda Medical College Hospital. What experts say is the ideal time to protect yourself Medical experts urge getting a flu shot soon, before influenza starts spreading widely — just remember it can take two weeks for protection to kick in. By Lauran Neergaard | The Associated Press • Published October 2, 2026 • Updated on October 2, 2026 at 1:33 pm BOOKMARKER 0:00 Play 0:00 / 1:49 Mute ShareToggle Fullscreen NBC Universal, Inc. Should you get your flu shot with a Covid vaccine? Here’s the guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It’s October and time for flu shots. Medical experts urge getting a flu vaccination soon, before influenza starts spreading widely — and to get up to date on protection against other fall respiratory viruses, too. Updated COVID-19 shots are available now, plus shots for people especially vulnerable to another winter risk called RSV. Stream Connecticut News for free, 24/7, wherever you are. WATCH HERE While these infections make many people feel miserable for a few days before they recover, every year flu alone causes hundreds of thousands of hospitalizations in the U.S. and kills tens of thousands. Vaccination isn’t “a guarantee that we’re going to prevent illness. But just like the seat belt in your car, it decreases risk” of the worst outcomes, said Dr. Ryan Stanton of the American College of Emergency Physicians. Fall vaccine advice usually comes from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and its independent advisory panel. But this year that panel, which influences state and insurance vaccine policies, is caught in a court battle and the CDC hasn't updated its advice. Now doctors’ groups are filling the gap: the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America have posted vaccination guidelines for their patient populations plus the scientific evidence behind them. Here's what to know: Just about everyone should get vaccinated against flu Just about everybody starting at age 6 months needs flu vaccination, the medical societies agree. But flu is particularly dangerous for people 65 and older, pregnant women, young children and people of any age who have chronic health problems, including asthma, diabetes, heart disease and weak immune systems. The last two flu seasons brought unusually high numbers of child deaths, the vast majority of them in unvaccinated kids. The vaccines don't block all flu infections, but they do help prevent the worst outcomes, decreasing older adults' hospitalizations by 31% last year, according to the Vaccine Integrity Project, a public health group based at the University of Minnesota. 1:34 Is it a cold or the flu? It’s cold and flu season again, which means you could be left wondering which virus is causing your symptoms. Here’s what you need to know. Here's how to pick from the multiple flu vaccine options Three “enhanced” flu vaccines are designed to better protect seniors. The American Academy of Family Physicians urges them to choose one — “but do not delay your vaccination if that one’s not available,” said AAFP’s Dr. Sarah Nosal. The Food and Drug Administration recently approved a new choice for people ages 50 and older, the first flu vaccine made with the same mRNA technology that was key to ending the COVID-19 pandemic. One study found Moderna's mFlusiva was 27% more effective against symptomatic illness among 50- to 64-year-olds than a standard shot. The shot-averse could choose a nasal spray, FluMist, if they're ages 2 to 49 and meet other health criteria. The latest on COVID-19 vaccines COVID-19 shots once were recommended for just about everyone by federal health agencies, but like last year, the FDA has only formally approved them for higher-risk people — those ages 65 and older or younger people with at least one health condition that increases their risk. Still, the family physicians recommend all adults get a COVID-19 vaccination, especially seniors and those with other risk factors. Adults 65 and older should get a fall dose and then a second dose six months later, as immunity wanes over time, Nosal said. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a COVID-19 shot for all children ages 6 months to 23 months, and for older kids with high-risk conditions. It also supports vaccination for any child whose parent wishes it. 0:54 CDC Approves COVID-19 Vaccines for Youngest Kids A Centers for Disease Control and Prevention advisory committee on Saturday endorsed Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna’s Covid-19 vaccines for young children, the last step before Director Dr. Rochelle Walensky can issue her final signoff. With millions of shots administered, there’s no evidence that coronavirus vaccination during pregnancy increases the risk of miscarriage or other problems, “so please get the vaccine,” said ACOG’s Dr. Christina Davidson. Depending on age, people can choose a shot from Moderna, Pfizer, or the only non-mRNA version from Novavax and Sanofi. Just like with flu vaccines, these shots are better at preventing severe disease than mild cases. The Vaccine Integrity Project said last fall’s COVID-19 shots cut the risk of hospitalization by 53% in seniors and slashed emergency room visits for very young children. Common side effects for flu and COVID-19 vaccines are mild and temporary, such as sore arms, fatigue, headaches, muscle aches, and mild fever. They occurred somewhat more often with the new mFlusiva than with standard flu shots. What to expect after ‘superflu' winter Vaccines Sep 18 The first mRNA flu shot is now available. Here's who can get it Here's where you can get vaccinated While pediatricians and some clinics offer both flu and coronavirus shots, they're most common in pharmacies. For COVID-19 shots, states have more pharmacy rules. For example, Walgreens says it offers those shots without a prescription in all but two states, Arizona and Oregon, but can provide doses for children as young as 3 in some states while others have higher age limits. Medicare covers the fall shots and most private health insurers say they plan to continue doing so through 2027. If you want to choose mFlusiva, the new Moderna flu option, make sure to double check that your insurance covers it. When to get vaccinated Flu experts say October is best, although vaccinations will remain available through the fall — just remember it can take two weeks for protection to kick in. COVID-19 cases rose in the late summer and usually do again around the winter holidays. Some experts say it's also OK to time the coronavirus shot a few weeks ahead of an event you wouldn’t want to miss because of illness, like a special trip or get-together. 0:51 Four Ways to Prevent Getting RSV What are preventative measures you can take to avoid RSV? The CDC recommends washing hands and avoiding close contact with others. RSV is a nuisance for many, but it can be deadly for some RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, typically is a cold-like nuisance during the fall, winter and early spring. But it can be severe, even life-threatening, for infants and older adults. The family physicians recommend a one-time vaccination for adults 75 and older, people 50 to 74 who are at increased risk, or younger people with weak immune systems. It’s also recommended during late pregnancy to protect infants born during RSV season. Separately, the pediatricians recommend a vaccine-like medication for those infants whose moms weren't vaccinated and some other high-risk babies. records.content: Experts say now is an ideal time to get a flu shot, before influenza starts spreading widely. It's October and time for flu shots.[br /][br /]Medical experts urge getting a flu vaccination soon, before influenza starts spreading widely — and to get up to date on protection against other fall respiratory viruses, too. Updated COVID-19 shots are available now, plus shots for people especially vulnerable to another winter risk called RSV.[br /][br /]While these infections make many people feel miserable for a few days before they recover, every year flu alone causes hundreds of thousands of hospitalizations in the U.S. and kills tens of thousands.[br /][br /]Vaccination isn't "a guarantee that we're going to prevent illness. But just like the seat belt in your car, it decreases risk" of the worst outcomes, said Dr. Ryan Stanton of the American College of Emergency Physicians.[br /][br /]Fall vaccine advice usually comes from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and its independent advisory panel. But this year that panel, which influences state and insurance vaccine policies, is caught in a court battle and the CDC hasn't updated its flu advice.[br /][br /]Now doctors' groups are filling the gap: the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America have posted vaccination guidelines for their patient populations plus the scientific evidence behind them.[br /][br /][b][u]Here's what to know:[/u][/b][br /][br /][h2]Just about everyone should get vaccinated against flu[/h2][br /][br /]Just about everybody starting at age 6 months needs flu vaccination, the medical societies agree. But flu is particularly dangerous for people 65 and older, pregnant women, young children and people of any age who have chronic health problems, including asthma, diabetes, heart disease and weak immune systems. The last two flu seasons brought unusually high numbers of child deaths, the vast majority of them in unvaccinated kids.[br /][br /]The vaccines don't block all flu infections, but they do help prevent the worst outcomes, decreasing older adults' hospitalizations by 31% last year, according to the Vaccine Integrity Project, a public health group based at the University of Minnesota.[br /][br /][h2]Here's how to pick from the multiple flu vaccine options[/h2][br /][br /]Three "enhanced" flu vaccines are designed to better protect seniors. The American Academy of Family Physicians urges them to choose one — "but do not delay your vaccination if that one's not available," said AAFP's Dr. Sarah Nosal.[br /][br /]The Food and Drug Administration recently approved a new choice for people ages 50 and older, the first flu vaccine made with the same mRNA technology that was key to ending the COVID-19 pandemic. One study found Moderna's mFlusiva was 27% more effective against symptomatic illness among 50- to 64-year-olds than a standard shot.[br /][br /]The shot-averse could choose a nasal spray, FluMist, if they're ages 2 to 49 and meet other health criteria.[br /][br /][h2]The latest on COVID-19 vaccines[/h2][br /][br /]COVID-19 shots once were recommended for just about everyone by federal health agencies, but like last year, the FDA has only formally approved them for higher-risk people — those ages 65 and older or younger people with at least one health condition that increases their risk.[br /][br /]Still, the family physicians recommend all adults get a COVID-19 vaccination, especially seniors and those with other risk factors. Adults 65 and older should get a fall dose and then a second dose six months later, as immunity wanes over time, Nosal said.[br /][br /]The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a COVID-19 shot for all children ages 6 months to 23 months, and for older kids with high-risk conditions. It also supports vaccination for any child whose parent wishes it.[br /][br /]With millions of shots administered, there's no evidence that coronavirus vaccination during pregnancy increases the risk of miscarriage or other problems, "so please get the vaccine," said ACOG's Dr. Christina Davidson.[br /][br /]Depending on age, people can choose a shot from Moderna, Pfizer, or the only non-mRNA version from Novavax and Sanofi.[br /][br /]Just like with flu vaccines, these shots are better at preventing severe disease than mild cases. The Vaccine Integrity Project said last fall's COVID-19 shots cut the risk of hospitalization by 53% in seniors and slashed emergency room visits for very young children.[br /][br /]Common side effects for flu and COVID-19 vaccines are mild and temporary, such as sore arms, fatigue, headaches, muscle aches, and mild fever. They occurred somewhat more often with the new mFlusiva than with standard flu shots.[br /][br /][h2]Here's where you can get vaccinated[/h2][br /][br /]While pediatricians and some clinics offer both flu and coronavirus shots, they're available for most ages through pharmacies. For example, Walgreens says it now offers both shots for ages 3 and older, no prescription needed.[br /][br /]Medicare covers the fall shots and most private health insurers say they plan to continue doing so through 2027. If you want to choose mFlusiva, the new Moderna flu option, make sure to double check that your insurance covers it.[br /][br /][h2]When to get vaccinated[/h2][br /][br /]Flu experts say October is best, although vaccinations will remain available through the fall — just remember it can take two weeks for protection to kick in. COVID-19 cases rose in the late summer and usually do again around the winter holidays. Some experts say it's also OK to time the coronavirus shot a few weeks ahead of an event you wouldn't want to miss because of illness, like a special trip or get-together.[br /][br /][h2]RSV is a nuisance for many, but it can be deadly for some[/h2][br /][br /]RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, typically is a cold-like nuisance during the fall, winter and early spring. But it can be severe, even life-threatening, for infants and older adults.[br /][br /]The family physicians recommend a one-time vaccination for adults 75 and older, people 50 to 74 who are at increased risk, or younger people with weak immune systems.[br /][br /]It's also recommended during late pregnancy to protect infants born during RSV season. Separately, the pediatricians recommend a vaccine-like medication for those infants whose moms weren't vaccinated and some other high-risk babies. Report a correction or typo

Sign Up Today My Account Dashboard Profile Saved items Logout Facebook Twitter YouTube Instagram News Weather Sports Watch Video Contests Deals Contact 9 News Download Our Apps Check The Forecast State health officials recommend vaccines before respiratory illnesses pick up By John Burton Oct 1, 2026 Oct 1, 2026 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save (WXPR) - Respiratory illnesses tend to start picking up as we move into fall. State Epidemiologist Dr. Ryan Westergaard says you don’t need to wait for virus activity to increase to take action. “Vaccines remain one of the best ways to reduce the risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death from these respiratory viruses, and they are available right now,” said Westergaard. “We know that people are balancing work and family, busy schedules, and that finding the time to get vaccinated can be challenging, so vaccines are available in other settings beyond a traditional doctor's office, including through pharmacies, local health departments, and community vaccination clinics.” Some people may feel they are healthy and wouldn’t suffer too badly from the flu. Westergaard says there are still benefits to the community from getting vaccinated. “Number one, the chance of getting severely ill is significantly lower. And the benefit to our community and for our healthcare system is that the more people we can protect from serious influenza and COVID, the less strain it puts on our hospital systems, having to take care of people with severe respiratory illness.” Most health insurance plans continue to cover recommended vaccines, although coverage can vary. The Department of Health Services recommends vaccines for flu, COVID-19, and RSV, if people are eligible. During the 2025-2026 season, Wisconsin saw nearly 11,000 hospitalizations associated with complications of flu, RSV, and COVID-19, with the majority occurring in older adults. DHS recommends the following immunization guidance for the upcoming respiratory virus season: Flu (influenza): Flu vaccines are updated every year to offer the best protection against the viruses predicted to circulate. A flu vaccine is recommended each flu season for everyone 6 months and older. This is especially important for people at highest risk of severe illness including older adults, people with chronic health conditions, people who are pregnant, and young children, as well as those who interact with high-risk individuals. COVID-19: COVID vaccines are updated to help offer the best protection against current variants. An updated COVID-19 vaccine is recommended every fall for all Wisconsinites 6 months and older. This is especially important for people 65 and older, people who have never received a COVID-19 vaccine, and people who are at risk for severe complications from COVID-19, including infants and young children, people who are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or who have recently given birth, and people with underlying health conditions. People who spend time with these populations should also be vaccinated against COVID-19 to reduce their likelihood of spreading the disease. RSV: A one-time dose of RSV vaccination for those who are over age 50 and at increased risk of severe RSV disease, and for all adults 75 and older. The RSV vaccine is not a vaccine that older adults need to get every year. DHS also recommends one dose of the vaccine be given during 32-36 weeks of pregnancy, between September 1 and March 1. If the RSV vaccine isn't given during pregnancy, an RSV antibody shot is recommended for infants less than 8 months old and some toddlers to protect them from severe RSV disease. The RSV vaccine can be given at the same time as other vaccines, including COVID-19 and flu. To find and schedule a vaccine, Wisconsin residents are encouraged to check with their primary care provider, local or Tribal health department, pharmacy, or community clinic. DHS has issued statewide standing orders for flu and COVID-19 vaccines that allow most Wisconsinites who want them to get vaccines at pharmacies across the state without a prescription. Most health insurance plans continue to cover recommended vaccines, although coverage can vary. Wisconsinites should consult their insurance provider to learn about coverage options. Anyone who does not have health insurance, or whose health insurance does not cover vaccines, can connect with the Vaccines for Children Program and Vaccines for Adults Program. Both programs will provide access to flu and COVID vaccines. Find more information about respiratory viruses on the DHS Respiratory Viruses webpage. Public health officials consider the first week of October to be the unofficial start of respiratory virus season, since influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) activity typically increase during this period. A recording of the media briefing is available on OHA’s YouTube channel. Sidelinger underscored the importance of getting vaccinated now by noting that Oregon has seen an increase in positive flu tests in recent weeks, with percent positivity at 3.2%. He said flu transmission remains low, but “that could change quickly and we are recommending that people in Oregon seek their flu shots soon.” A summer 2026 surge in COVID-19 activity—a pattern seen annually since 2021—has leveled off, although it’s not clear if the increase has yet peaked. “With elevated COVID-19 spread, it is a great time to update COVID-19 protection,” Sidelinger said. The physicians also discussed the ongoing measles outbreak during the briefing. Sidelinger emphasized that measles is widespread in Oregon. With 58 cases in the state as of Monday, the state now has the highest number of measles cases in the state since 1991, when we had 93 cases, and since measles was declared eliminated in 2000. That is a sobering statistic, Sidelinger said, particularly when understanding that 96% of those measles cases were in unvaccinated persons or individuals whose vaccine status was unknown. The risk of severe disease from measles for people who are vaccinated is very low. Measles spreads rapidly in unvaccinated communities and anyone who is unvaccinated is at risk. For children, two doses of MMR vaccine given after a child’s first birthday are recommended. Adults who do not have records of getting two MMR—or measles—vaccines, can talk to their health care provider about their level of immunity, including whether they would benefit from an MMR vaccine at this time when measles is circulating in Oregon. Dawn Nolt, M.D., MPH, professor of pediatric infectious diseases at OHSU’s Doernbecher Children’s Hospital, said that while every respiratory virus season brings illness, “we have an opportunity to make the 2026-2027 season less severe for our children, families and communities” by getting vaccinated sooner than later. “We want our kids to be where they belong: in school, with their friends, with their families, and making memories—not in bed sick or in a hospital,” Nolt said. Leona O’Keefe, M.D., medical director of clinical services at Jackson Care Connect in Jackson County, recalled once caring for a young father who spent weeks in the intensive care unit and hospital with flu. He was not vaccinated because, like many busy parents, he felt he didn’t have time available in his schedule. “I’ve supported family members through fear and sadness around these preventable diseases,” O’Keefe said. She added, “I would be devastated if one of my children was harmed by a preventable disease because I chose not to vaccinate them, whereas I would be far more able to face myself if I gave my children incredibly safe vaccines that hold such low risks.” O’Keefe also noted that prevention can be especially important in rural communities, where families may live far from hospitals or specialists and serious illness can require long travel times and cause additional stress for patients and caregivers. As the 2026–2027 respiratory virus season begins, Nolt highlighted three recommendations for families: 1. Get vaccinated and keep your family’s vaccines up to date. Vaccines against COVID-19, flu, RSV, and measles can dramatically reduce the risk of serious illness and hospitalization. 2. Take simple steps to reduce the spread of infection. Respiratory viruses spread easily, especially indoors, and measles is extraordinarily contagious. Stay home when you’re sick, wash your hands, cover your coughs and sneezes, and consider masking when respiratory viruses are circulating widely or someone in your household is particularly vulnerable. 3. Know who is most vulnerable and act early. Everyone can get infected, but infants, older adults, and people with certain underlying health conditions are at greater risk of serious complications if they get sick. Encourages Older Adults to Talk to Their Healthcare Provider About RSV Vaccination News provided by American Lung Association Oct 01, 2026, 12:12 ET Share this article Share toX Share this article Share toX CHICAGO, Oct. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, the American Lung Association launched a new campaign to urge older adults and people with pre-existing conditions to talk with their healthcare provider about getting vaccinated against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). RSV is highly contagious and spreads widely during the fall and winter months, like many other respiratory viruses, and can infect people of all ages. While most people develop only mild symptoms, infants and older adults can get very sick. Severe complications from RSV include pneumonia, worsening of an existing chronic medical condition like asthma, COPD or heart failure. In older adults, severe RSV illness can negatively impact quality of life and cause a loss of independence due to long-lasting symptoms that decrease one's ability to carry out daily activities. "RSV poses a significant public health burden in the U.S. Unfortunately, each year, the disease leads to an estimated 180,000 hospitalizations among adults ages 50 and older. During the 2025-26 season, RSV contributed to as many as 25,000 deaths across all ages," said Harold Wimmer, President and CEO of the American Lung Association. "Heading into the holiday season, it is critical for older adults and people living with chronic lung disease to take steps to protect themselves from RSV, including by discussing RSV vaccination with a healthcare provider." Adults who are at increased risk of RSV complications include those age 75 and older; adults with chronic lung or heart disease such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), interstitial lung disease (ILD) or congestive heart failure; adults with weakened immune systems; and adults living in nursing homes. Current guidance from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommend a single dose of RSV vaccine for eligible adults. It is not an annual vaccine. Adults who have already received one dose, including in a prior year, should not receive another dose at this time. However, adults can get vaccinated for RSV at any time of the year. RSV, flu and COVID-19 vaccines can be received during the same visit, depending on availability. Vaccination coverage rates are low, and many adults who are at increased risk have not discussed RSV vaccination with a healthcare provider to help prevent serious illness. As of February 22, 2026, 43% of adults 75 years and older and 33% of adults 50─74 years with a high-risk condition for RSV reported having ever received an RSV vaccine, leaving many eligible adults without vaccination protection. Hispanic and Latino adults experience significantly lower vaccination rates. The American Lung Association encourages adults to speak with to their healthcare provider about staying up to date on all recommended respiratory vaccinations, including an RSV vaccine if eligible. For more information on RSV prevention and vaccination, visit Lung.org/rsv. This initiative is supported by an educational grant from GSK. About the American Lung Association The American Lung Association is the leading organization working to save lives by improving lung health and preventing lung disease through education, advocacy and research. The work of the American Lung Association is focused on four strategic imperatives: to defeat lung cancer; to champion clean air for all; to improve the quality of life for those with lung disease and their families; and to create a tobacco-free future. The latest numbers from the federal government show flu season has arrived, with an increase in cases and cold symptoms. According to the Canadian respiratory virus surveillance report published Friday, the number of positive tests “has been increasing” in recent weeks, with COVID-19 seeing a 3.8 per cent spike and influenza at 3.7. The federal government’s FluWatchers program also saw a 1.5 per cent increase in reported cough and fever symptoms. However, the report said the number of cases remains at “very low levels” and varies by region. Meanwhile, positive tests for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are “stable at interseasonal levels” at 0.2 per cent. The report includes data from the week ending Sept. 26. Flu season cough fever COVID-19 Federal government data found that more people getting COVID-19, influenza as well as the cough and fever, as of Sept. 26, 2026. (Pexels) Dr. Isaac Bogoch, an infectious diseases specialist at Toronto General Hospital, said the data isn’t surprising. “We know that there’s going to be a rise in respiratory viruses as we move throughout the fall. We’re already starting to see the very earliest signs of that, especially with COVID and with influenza,” Bogoch said in a video interview with CTVNews.ca on Friday. “And of course, we don’t need a crystal ball to predict the future. We know that we’re going to see more and more of these viruses, and ultimately, we’ll start to see RSV as well come into the mix.” The percentage of positive cases for other respiratory viruses are “following historically observed trends,” the report said. The viruses with the highest number of cases are enteroviruses (EV) and rhinoviruses (RV), which are continuing to rise. Bogoch said EV and RV are “very common viral infections” that can cause upper respiratory tract infections or gastrointestinal illness. Among the 52 laboratory-confirmed respiratory viral outbreaks, the majority were associated with COVID-19 at 67.31 per cent. The majority of positive tests for both COVID-19 (63 per cent) and influenza (55 per cent) came from those aged 65 and older, while more than half of RSV cases (52 per cent) were from those four years old and under. Bogoch said Canada will probably have “a flu season just like we’ve had just about every other year,” but he recommends people still take precautions to protect themselves and others from infections. He said getting vaccinated, staying home when you’re sick, wearing masks and improving the air quality indoors are ways to reduce the risk of getting sick. “We know what the tools are to get through another respiratory virus season, and we’ll get through this one like we’ve been through many in the past,” Bogoch said. Baker Opens in new window and Krista Sharpe-Kilpatrick Opens in new window Published: October 06, 2026 at 5:22p.m. EDT Pharmacists are reporting an early start to the cold and flu season. CTV’s Krista Sharpe-Kilpatrick reports. Cold and flu season has arrived early in Waterloo-Wellington. The peak period is usually between November and April, but cases are already popping up across the community. The Region of Waterloo’s Respiratory Illness Dashboard, which was last updated on Sept. 26, showed a weekly average of 1.3 patients had been hospitalized for the flu. For COVID-19, the average was 5.1. According to the dashboard for Wellington-Dufferin-Guelph Public Health, the most recent data showed an average of 0.04 flu patients per week and 0.70 COVID-19 illnesses as of Sept. 26. Neither have seen any cases of Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) during that same time period. Hospitalizations, it must be noted, reflect only the most severe cases. As many people won’t report milder symptoms, it is nearly impossible to determine the true number of illnesses throughout Waterloo-Wellington. “Until we start getting more data with more cases and we know a little bit more,” said David Aoki, Waterloo Region’s director of infectious diseases and chief nursing officer. “It’s still very early. And there’s nothing to indicate that this year is going to be anything worse than what we’ve seen in the past.” Vaccine availability Free flu and COVID-19 vaccines will be widely available soon. “At the Region of Waterloo, we’re starting to offer our clinics for high-risk people starting next week,” said Aoki. “Then we’ll have our public clinics during the week of Oct. 26.” Appointments with public health can be booked online. Wellington-Dufferin-Guelph Public Health will start rolling out their vaccine clinics on Oct. 13. Appointments can be booked by telephone or through public health’s online portal. Pharmacies also offer vaccines. While some accept walk-ins, others, due to the limited availability of the shots, may require pre-booked appointments. Connie Phillion, a pharmacist at the Doon Mills Guardian Pharmacy, said she expects flu shots to arrive sometime between Oct. 13 and Oct. 26. Only then can she start booking appointments for anyone considered high-risk, including older adults and those with underlying health conditions. Preventing illness is just one reason to get vaccinated. Another is that it protects everyone else around you. “For those of you who do get sick, don’t go out and spread it to others,” advised Dr. Nicola Mercer, the medical officer of health for Wellington-Dufferin-Guelph. “Try and stay home, get well. records.content: As the leaves start to turn and autumn settles in, a familiar but serious concern is again at the forefront for communities across North America: the arrival of respiratory virus season. This fall, the convergence of influenza, Covid-19, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) has prompted health officials and medical organizations in both the United States and Canada to roll out updated vaccination campaigns, offering new guidance in the face of evolving viral threats and shifting federal oversight. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and corroborated by CNN and Mezha , seasonal influenza activity is currently low at the national level. However, certain regions, particularly Washington state's King County, have seen a noticeable uptick in emergency department visits for flu since mid-August 2026. The CDC has responded by posting guidance online that largely follows last year’s recommendations for flu and Covid-19 vaccines. This comes as the agency navigates changes to its vaccine advisory committee and ongoing legal challenges, which have complicated the release of new, unified federal vaccine guidance. Amid this uncertainty, independent reviews of the 2026-27 vaccine formulations were published in September in the journal JAMA . These reviews, led by the American Medical Association and the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project, have informed updated recommendations from a coalition of medical groups, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America. Dr. Bruce Gellin, board chair of the Vaccine Integrity Project and professor of medicine at Georgetown University, emphasized the ongoing necessity for clear, evidence-based guidance. “Unfortunately today, the federal government is not fulfilling that responsibility in the way that it historically has. But the need for that work has not disappeared. Influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and the RSV viruses will circulate again this fall and winter,” Gellin said at a news briefing, as reported by CNN . He added, “We cannot allow the breakdown of a federal process to create a vacuum in evidence-based vaccine guidance.” For Americans and Canadians alike, access to vaccines is robust this year. Flu, Covid-19, and RSV immunizations are available at most major pharmacies, and, reassuringly, insurers have indicated that they will cover these respiratory virus immunizations. Dr. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, noted, “Vaccines are one of medicine’s greatest success stories. They prevent serious illness, reduce hospitalizations and long-term complications and save lives.” She stressed that the 2026-27 recommendations are grounded in the latest evidence and shaped by what physicians are seeing in their practices. North of the border, the government of New Brunswick has launched a province-wide respiratory illness prevention campaign, announcing that updated influenza and Covid-19 vaccines will be available for free to everyone aged six months and older starting October 13, 2026. As reported by the Fredericton Independent , Dr. Yves Léger, New Brunswick’s chief medical officer of health, stated, “If you are eligible for both, we encourage you to get them at the same visit.” He highlighted that these vaccines reduce the chance of serious illness, hospitalization, and community spread. Appointments can be scheduled through the government’s website or by contacting participating community pharmacies, and select primary care providers will also have doses available. Special attention is being paid to high-risk groups, including those aged 65 and older, residents of long-term care facilities, individuals with chronic health conditions, and pregnant women. For children who are averse to injections, the province is offering FluMist, a nasal spray influenza vaccine, for those aged two to seventeen. Families are encouraged to check eligibility and book appointments through their healthcare providers or local public health offices. So, who should get which vaccine, and when? The updated guidance is clear but nuanced. For RSV, recommendations cover several groups. According to the American Academy of Pediatrics and echoed by Mezha , older adults—specifically people aged 50 and older with high-risk conditions, and everyone over 75—should receive one dose. This is not an annual shot; one dose should protect recipients for the entire season. Pregnant individuals are advised to get the maternal RSV vaccine, Abrysvo, between September 1 and March 1, reflecting a shift in timing due to a later and more severe RSV season. Infants younger than eight months should receive an RSV monoclonal antibody unless their mother was vaccinated during pregnancy. Children between eight and nineteen months who are at high risk should also receive the monoclonal antibody, and immunosuppressed adults are likewise advised to get a single dose. For flu, the message is straightforward: everyone six months and older should get an annual flu shot. Adults 65 and older are encouraged to opt for an enhanced vaccine—high-dose, adjuvanted, or recombinant—when available, but should not delay vaccination if these are not in stock. Notably, for the first time in 2026, an mRNA-based flu vaccine is available for adults 50 and older. Pregnant people are recommended to receive the inactivated or recombinant influenza vaccine, not the nasal spray, as per the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. Dr. Christina Davidson of ACOG explained, “Pregnant and postpartum people still have a significantly higher risk of developing serious complications from infection compared with non-pregnant people.” She also noted the added benefit that vaccination during pregnancy can confer immunity to the newborn. October is widely regarded as the optimal time to get the flu shot, ensuring protection throughout the peak of the season. Providers use the catchy slogan “flu before boo” to remind patients to get vaccinated before Halloween. The updated Covid-19 vaccines are recommended for adults, especially those over 19, and particularly for people 65 and older, who should receive a second dose six months after the initial one to maintain protection. Infants between six and twenty-three months, children in high-risk groups, and immunocompromised individuals aged six months and older are also prioritized. Pregnant and breastfeeding people are strongly advised to get the Covid-19 vaccine as well. Dr. Davidson stressed, “A recommendation for the Covid vaccine is based on more than five years of research and millions of administered doses. I want to emphasize that the evidence has found no increased risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth or birth defects.” For those who have recently recovered from Covid-19, experts advise waiting four to six months before getting the updated vaccine. As Dr. Sandra Adamson Fryhofer of the American Medical Association put it, “You’re going to get your most protection in those first few months after the vaccine. So if you have a big event—if you have to go to a wedding, or if you’re going on some fabulous trip, or you’re going to a fabulous birthday party, or just any birthday party or get-together—think about getting that vaccine a couple of weeks before that event, so you’ll stay healthy and well.” In both the U.S. and Canada, vaccines are available at most major pharmacies, covered by insurance, and, for children, accessible through federal programs like Vaccines for Children. Information and booking resources are readily available on government websites, making it as easy as possible for families to get protected. This fall, as the air grows crisp and routines shift, public health experts are urging everyone to take advantage of these updated vaccines. With a clear roadmap from medical organizations and support from local governments, communities have the tools to stay healthy and keep respiratory viruses at bay.
